france24fr.description: Maude Petit-Jové, notre correspondante à Madrid, analyse la situation.

france24fr.description: La canicule s'est installée jeudi sur une large partie de la France, de Paris au centre-est, et s'étendra vendredi, avec une cinquantaine de départements en vigilance orange, et plusieurs municipalités annulant la populaire Fête de la musique prévue dimanche.

france24fr.title: Bombardements de Moscou : quand l'Ukraine veut priver la Russie de son or noir
france24fr.description: L’attaque massive de drones menée par l'armée ukrainienne contre la capitale russe visait tout particulièrement la raffinerie de Moscou et s’inscrit dans une campagne intense de bombardements des infrastructures pétrolières russes. Un levier de plus en plus coûteux pour le Kremlin, qui vise à saper sa capacité à financer son effort de guerre.

france24fr.description: Emmanuel Viver, co-fondateur de HUB INSTITUTE, est notre invité.

france24fr.description: Pour les démocrates, le texte de l'accord de paix signé par Donald Trump ne change rien sur le fond.

france24fr.title: Le Niger repousse une nouvelle attaque contre l'aéroport de Niamey
france24fr.description: Pierre Donadieu, Journaliste AFP en Afrique de l'ouest, est notre invité.

france24fr.title: Signature surprise de l'accord Iran/Etats-Unis par Trump à Versailles
france24fr.description: Le protocole d'accord, qui inclut le front libanais, a été signé par Donald Trump, en visite en France. "Je viens de le signer", a-t-il dit à la presse en quittant le château de Versailles. Un responsable de la Maison Blanche a par la suite publié une vidéo sur X où l'on voit le républicain signer l'accord aux côtés d'Emmanuel Macron, le pouce levé et sourire aux lèvres.

france24fr.title: Musée du Quai Branly : 25 millions de visiteurs en 20 ans
france24fr.description: Vingt ans après son inauguration par Jacques Chirac, le Musée du Quai Branly-Jacques Chirac célèbre un anniversaire symbolique. Devenu l'un des grands musées français consacrés aux arts et civilisations d'Afrique, d'Asie, d'Océanie et des Amériques, il revendique plus de 25 millions de visiteurs. Mais cet anniversaire est aussi l'occasion d'évoquer les questions de restitution des œuvres, de provenance des collections et de dialogue avec les communautés concernées. france24fr.title: Kenya : le président William Ruto au sommet du G7 sur invitation de la France
france24fr.description:
Au sommet du G7 qui a pris fin ce mercredi, le président kényan William Ruto a porté la voix de l'Afrique sur la scène internationale.
 
Invité par la France, il a participé aux échanges aux côtés du président égyptien Abdel Fattah al-Sissi.
 
Une présence remarquée dans un sommet marqué par l'absence de l'Afrique du Sud.

france24fr.title: Les fortes chaleurs en France poussent plusieurs villes à annuler la Fête de la musique
france24fr.description: Alors que la France est à nouveau en proie à une vague de chaleur avec des températures flirtant à certains endroits avec les 40°C, plusieurs villes ont décidé d'annuler les événements prévus pour la Fête de la musique.

france24fr.title: Mondial 2026 : la résilience de Yoane Wissa, cinq ans après une agression à l'acide
france24fr.description: Cinq ans après avoir failli perdre la vue suite à une agression à l’acide, Yoane Wissa a montré toute sa résilience en égalisant contre le Portugal sur la plus grande des scènes de football. La RD Congo peut remercier son attaquant qui est venu récompenser une très belle prestation collective.

france24fr.title: Canicule à Paris : canaux et piscines pris d'assaut face aux fortes chaleurs
france24fr.description: Face aux fortes chaleurs, Paris a autorisé la baignade dans une portion du canal Saint-Martin, dans l'est de la capitale, pour en faire un "véritable outil de rafraîchissement". "Profitez-en, et faites attention à vous avec la chaleur", a lancé le maire PS, Emmanuel Grégoire, dans un message sur X montrant des foules en maillot de bain plongeant à la recherche d'un peu de fraîcheur.

france24fr.title: VivaTech à Paris : le sommet de la Start-up Nation fête ses 10 ans
france24fr.description: Gilles Babinet, entrepreneur et président de la Mission Café IA, est notre invité.

zeit.description: Neue Wohnungen entstehen häufig nicht dort, wo sie gebraucht werden. Das klingt nach Marktversagen. Der wahre Grund ist viel einfacher – und umso schwerer zu beheben.

observador.description: Equipamentos para bloquear telemóveis e drones na prisão de onde fugiram cinco reclusos em setembro de 2024 chegaram depois de atrasos ligados a Israel.

observador.description: Os suspeitos, detidos terça-feira pela GNR, ficam proibidos de contactar vítimas e familiares e de exercer funções de cuidadores. Investigação terá estado parada um ano no DCIAP.

observador.title: Lutar para não perder alguém ou lutar para o merecer?
observador.description: A diferença entre as duas coisas não é pequena. Numa, o motor é o medo de ficar sem o outro; na outra, o desejo de estar à altura. E há ainda um terceiro lugar, o pior de todos: lutar para conquistar

observador.title: Agressor do ator Adérito Lopes continua sob investigação
observador.description: Um ano depois, caso das agressões ao ator Adérito Lopes, no Teatro A Barraca, continua em investigação. Inquérito está em segredo de justiça e só "recentemente" é que advogados acederam ao processo.

observador.title: Centenas contra pacote laboral junto ao parlamento
observador.description: Centenas de trabalhadores em frente ao Palácio de São Bento gritam: "Não vamos desistir, o pacote é para cair". O PCP e o BE marcaram também a sua presença no protesto antes do início da sessão.

observador.title: Advogada constituída arguida em investigação a imigrantes
observador.description: GNR apreendeu procurações e autos de extravio no escritório. Esquema permitia ocultar data de entrada em Portugal para facilitar legalização. Investigação, que dura há um ano, partiu de uma queixa.

observador.description: As notícias na Rádio Observador. Aconteça o que acontecer.

observador.title: Grupo acusado de planear atentado contra Montenegro
observador.description: Movimento Armilar Lusitano tinha longa lista de "alvos e ameaças" e chegou a reunir informação sobre a morada e o policiamento da casa do primeiro-ministro.

observador.title: PSP do Porto diz estar a tentar perceber queixas da DCI
observador.description: Sindicato convocou concentração para 13 de julho. Polícias da DIC do Porto acusam comando de os obrigar a piquetes e prevenções sem compensação.

observador.title: PJ detém dois suspeitos de 50 burlas informáticas
observador.description: Os dois detidos, com idades entre os 23 e os 27 anos, vendiam a terceiros equipamento e conhecimentos para executar fraudes em massa por SMS.

observador.title: Israel insiste em não sair do Líbano
observador.description: Apesar do memorando assinado, Israel não recua e diz que tropas "continuarão a reforçar a defesa dos residentes no norte de Israel". Nova ronda de negociação com o Líbano decorre na próxima semana.

observador.title: GNR apanha trio a descarregar haxixe em Aljezur
observador.description: A GNR especificou que os homens, com idades entre 28 e 43 anos, foram surpreendidos quando transferiam a droga de uma embarcação de alta velocidade (EAV) para viaturas de mercadorias.

observador.title: Rutte satisfeito com críticas de Hegseth aos aliados
observador.description: Hegseth acusou de "vergonhoso" o bloqueio de bases europeias e anunciou revisão da presença militar dos EUA na Europa em seis meses. Líder da NATO apoiou as críticas do secretário da Defesa dos EUA.

observador.title: Mãe e criança com Ébola raptadas de hospital
observador.description: O rapto de dois doentes com Ébola num hospital do leste da RD Congo volta a expor a desconfiança comunitária na saúde. Paradeiro das vítimas é desconhecido, mas as buscas continuam.

observador.title: Quase um milhão de palestinianos enfrenta calor em tendas
observador.description: Com 76,6% das casas destruídas ou danificadas e temperaturas a subir, cerca de 850 mil palestinianos estão sem acesso a materiais básicos de abrigo em Gaza.

observador.title: Faltam profissionais qualificados nas bibliotecas e arquivo
observador.description: Há duas décadas que não há formação na área de biblioteca e arquivo. "Profissionais que temos são muito poucos. Andamos a roubar profissionais a outros serviços", revela a Direção-Geral do Livro.

observador.title: IA consumirá 8% da eletricidade mundial em 2050
observador.description: Relatório da OPEP aponta IA como um dos maiores motores do crescimento da procura global de energia. Amazon, Google e Microsoft apostam no nuclear para responder.

observador.title: Irlanda acaba com três dias de espera para aborto
observador.description: Maioria dos deputados do Fianna Fáil e do Fine Gael, partidos no poder, votou contra o fim dos três dias obrigatórios antes do aborto. Diz que tempo de espera permite refletir sobre decisão.

spiegel.title: News des Tages: Brandmauer, Drohnenangriff auf Moskau, Hitze in Deutschland
spiegel.description: Nach einem Tabubruch im EU-Parlament kocht die Brandmauer-Debatte wieder hoch. Die Ukraine feiert einen dreifach wichtigen Militärschlag. Und im Spaßbad lauert eine unterschätzte Gefahr. Das ist die Lage am Donnerstagabend.

spiegel.title: Evonik streicht mehr als 2000 Stellen in Deutschland
spiegel.description: Der Chemiekonzern Evonik steckt seit Jahren tief in der Krise. Nun sollen in Deutschland und international erneut Tausende Jobs wegfallen, wenn auch ohne betriebsbedingte Kündigungen.

spiegel.description: Rechtsextremisten skandieren im Europaparlament, nachdem die sogenannte Rückführungsrichtlinie beschlossen wurde. Das zeigt, auf welchem Irrweg die Politik der Union unterwegs ist.

spiegel.title: Bergkarabach-Konflikt: Gerichtshof für Menschenrechte verurteilt Aserbaidschan wegen Folter
spiegel.description: Aserbaidschan muss 90.000 Euro an die Familie eines Armeniers zahlen, der im Jahr 2016 auf brutalste Weise gefoltert und anschließend getötet worden ist. Das entschied der Europäische Gerichtshof für Menschenrechte.

spiegel.title: HPV-Impfung senkt Risiko für Tod durch Gebärmutterhalskrebs auf nahezu null
spiegel.description: Krebserkrankungen des Gebärmutterhalses sind fast immer auf HPV-Infektionen zurückzuführen: Viren, die sexuell übertragbar sind. Dagegen gibt es eine Impfung. Studiendaten aus England zeigen, wie gut sie wirkt.

spiegel.description: Eine Kampfdrohne trifft eine Ölraffinerie, dann fliegt ein Stahldach durch die Luft: Videos zeigen die ukrainischen Luftangriffe auf Moskau. Die Menschen spüren die Folgen an der Tankstelle.

spiegel.description: Beim G7-Gipfel in Évian gab sich US-Präsident Donald Trump noch konziliant. Einen Tag später macht sein Verteidigungsminister den Bündnispartnern drei Wochen vor dem Nato-Treffen drastische Ansagen.

spiegel.description: Im EU-Parlament haben Konservative und extrem Rechte eine härtere Abschiebepolitik durchgesetzt. Schon im Plenum gab es Tumulte, nun sorgt eine angeblich lautstarke Feier nach der Abstimmung für Aufregung.

spiegel.title: Autolack: Forscher entwickeln ultraschwarze Farbe
spiegel.description: Chinesische Forscher haben eine Farbe entwickelt, die 99,9 Prozent des einfallenden Lichts schluckt – und als extrem dunkler Autolack taugen soll.

spiegel.title: Arbeitszeitgesetz: Entwurf aus dem Ministerium löst Streit mit Union aus
spiegel.description: Ein Entwurf für die Reform des Arbeitszeitgesetzes sorgt für mächtig Ärger. Die Union fühlt sich von Arbeitsministerin Bas verschaukelt, die sagt, sie sei noch gar nicht fertig. Die SPD aber verteidigt den Entwurf bereits.

spiegel.title: Fußball-WM heute: Das sollten Sie vor den Spielen am Abend und in der Nacht wissen
spiegel.description: Die Schweiz steht vor dem zweiten Gruppenspiel unter Druck, Tschechien hofft auf Tore von Patrick Schick. Und: Zwei Gastgeber kämpfen um den Einzug in die K.-o.-Runde. Alles Wichtige erfahren Sie hier.

spiegel.description: Für bestellte Coronamasken muss der Bund Nachzahlungen in Millionenhöhe leisten. Ein aktueller Fall zeigt, wie ihm die Zinsen davonlaufen.

spiegel.description: Sahra Wagenknecht stichelt gegen die Thüringer Brombeerkoalition – und wirbt für die Einbeziehung der AfD. Die BSW-Gründerin buhlt um die Stimmen der Brandmauer-Gegner im Osten. Kann die Strategie für sie aufgehen?

spiegel.description: Seit Jahren eskaliert die Drogenkriminalität in Ecuador, statistisch wird jeden Tag ein Mensch ermordet. Die Todesumstände von Carlos Suástegui schockieren aber selbst die Ecuadorianer.

new-sci.description: Defying the laws of thermodynamics, experiments are beginning to show that a quantum state that is frozen forever might not be impossible. If we can tame it, it could unlock whole new types of matter

new-sci.title: Carl Sagan's The Demon-Haunted World is still supremely relevant today
new-sci.description: Beautifully written, this guide to distinguishing between truth, misinformation and lies, first published in 1995, remains an essential read for anyone who considers themselves a critical thinker, says Leah Crane

new-sci.title: Complex life on Earth may last 500 million years longer than expected
new-sci.description: As the sun expands over the coming billions of years, Earth will become inhospitable to any life more complex than a microbe – but that might take longer than we thought

new-sci.title: New Scientist recommends an excellent look at the future of work
new-sci.description: Sarah O'Connor's We Are Not Machines explores how we are contorting ourselves to fit AI into our working lives – and what to do about it, finds Tom Knowles

new-sci.title: Ancient monument marked summer solstice centuries before Stonehenge
new-sci.description: Archaeologists have discovered traces of a wooden structure built 5000 years ago, 5 kilometres from Stonehenge, which appears to have been an even older monument for marking the summer solstice

new-sci.title: Cervical cancer deaths have plummeted thanks to HPV vaccine
new-sci.description: We already know the vaccine against human papillomavirus, or HPV, greatly reduces infections and cases of cervical cancer, and now we have the first evidence it prevents deaths too

new-sci.title: Chilling the body with drugs could limit brain damage from stroke
new-sci.description: Putting brain cells into a hibernation-like state via drugs that cool down core body temperature may help to preserve them following a stroke

new-sci.title: Oldest known plague outbreak killed hunter-gatherer children
new-sci.description: DNA evidence shows that plague bacteria devastated a community in Siberia more than 5000 years ago, challenging the idea that there were no major disease outbreaks before the advent of farming and large settlements

new-sci.title: Pigeons lock their eyes in place when they are flying
new-sci.description: Bird-mounted headsets and backpacks have revealed the surprising things pigeons do with their eyes when on the wing

new-sci.title: Our brains have their first thoughts surprisingly early in life
new-sci.description: By the time we’re born, our brains have all the hardware in place to form thoughts, and possibly even some conscious awareness

new-sci.title: Autism and ADHD are on the rise due to widening diagnostic criteria
new-sci.description: A study of 140,000 people suggests that a broadening of the diagnostic criteria for autism and ADHD explains the sharp rise in diagnoses, but that doesn't mean too many people are being told they are autistic or have ADHD

new-sci.title: Autism may have two distinct subtypes that vary by brain activity
new-sci.description: Evidence is mounting that there are distinct subtypes of autism, and now, scientists have found that the condition can vary according to the strength of people's brain connections

new-sci.title: The secrets to keeping your brain sharp in old age
new-sci.description: Neuroscientist Emily Rogalski studies superagers – people in their 80s or 90s with unusually keen memories, whose lifestyles suggest ways to slow cognitive decline

new-sci.title: Walking shark found in Papua New Guinea is new to science
new-sci.description: Hemiscyllium dudgeonae is the tenth recorded species of walking shark, which use their pectoral fins to move across reef flats, and its limited range means it may be at high risk of extinction

new-sci.title: Sperm have been made magnetic to allow IVF inside the body
new-sci.description: IVF could be done inside the body using a revolutionary technique that reduces the invasiveness of the traditional fertility treatment

new-sci.title: Arctic Ocean reaches tipping point that could be dire for marine life
new-sci.description: Disappearing sea ice is letting more sunlight in the Arctic Ocean and boosting phytoplankton growth, but this has depleted a crucial nutrient, which could severely affect animals higher up the food chain

new-sci.title: Technology is changing our perspective on nature – at every scale
new-sci.description: Inspired by Ariel Waldman’s docuseries Life Unearthed, columnist Annalee Newitz explores how microscopes, drones and specialised cameras are giving us an unprecedented view of nature from many different vantage points

new-sci.title: Has the answer to life's origins been hiding in our cells all along?
new-sci.description: The surprising discovery of mysterious blobs inside our cells is revolutionising our understanding of how life works, and how it got started

arxiv-ai.description:

arxiv-ai.description:
arXiv:2606.17339v1 Announce Type: new

arXiv:2606.17368v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models have accelerated the transition from passive conversational assistants to autonomous agents that can understand goals, plan actions, invoke tools, and execute multi-step tasks. arxiv-ai.description:

Abstract: Clinical decision support AI systems (CDSASs) must adapt to evolving patient conditions in real-time while adhering to strict safety constraints. arxiv-ai.description:
arXiv:2606.17443v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming a major way for consumers to find products, but we do not yet understand how brands compete in this new channel. We study brand dynamics in LLM recommendations using skincare products -- a category where consumers cannot easily judge quality before buying and must rely on brand reputation -- across three commercial LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, Claude Sonnet, Gemini 3 Flash), with a robustness check on search goods.

arxiv-ai.description:
arXiv:2606.17453v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly integrated into map services. arXiv:2606.17454v2 Announce Type: new

phys-org.title: Drivers of academic misconduct by professors and research students revealed
phys-org.description: Ensuring the research that we all rely on—whether for our health, environment or economy—is trustworthy is important for universities, governments and business. Unfortunately, academic misconduct is a growing concern, with researchers breaking the rules, such as making up results or copying others' work, making their research untrustworthy.

phys-org.title: Out-of-equilibrium cesium atoms reveal fractional Fermi seas, exposing new critical quantum phase
phys-org.description: In a new study published in Physical Review Letters, a team from the Nägerl group, together with theory collaborator Alvise Bastianello from the CNRS and the Université Paris-Dauphine, demonstrates that highly unusual quantum states known as "fractional Fermi seas" can be quantum engineered.

phys-org.title: From prejudice to harm—current policies targeting trans people follow a clear pattern of escalation
phys-org.description: Public debates about transgender issues are often framed as disagreements over evidence or safety. In my new article published in the International Journal of Transgender Health, I argue current policy shifts are better understood as part of a recognizable escalation pattern.

phys-org.title: How to train your magnet: Excitons as a new knob for magnetic control
phys-org.description: Scientists can learn a lot about a quantum material by watching how it responds to light. In magnetic semiconductors, one especially useful messenger is the exciton: a pairing of a negatively charged electron and the positively charged "hole" it leaves behind. Until now, excitons in magnetic materials have mostly been used as reporters. They could reveal how spins were arranged or how magnetic waves moved through a material. But Cornell researchers have shown that excitons can do more than obser

phys-org.title: Mystery of 17th century shipwreck holding 400 gold coins finally solved after 30 years
phys-org.description: The identity of a centuries-old shipwreck discovered off the south coast of England, holding 400 gold coins, has finally been identified as the Dutch trading ship "Dom van Keulen," which left Morocco for the Netherlands in the autumn of 1633.

phys-org.title: Shell too snug? Hermit crabs have a fix
phys-org.description: For decades, biologists have known that hermit crabs forced to live in shells that are too small slow their growth. What wasn't clear was how they did it. New research suggests the answer isn't simply that the crabs eat less. Instead, they appear to regulate growth by changing how efficiently they use the food they consume.

phys-org.title: Video: The economic pressures that are driving Californians to leave home
phys-org.description: Millions of Californians, in every part of the state, live with an uneasy day-to-day preoccupation: Housing is so expensive here, food and gas and utilities are so expensive—would it make sense to pull up stakes and leave for another state?

phys-org.title: What if there is no one to farm? Scientists reveal a hidden risk to future food security
phys-org.description: The cause of future food shortages may not be a lack of farmland, but a shortage of agricultural workers. Amid low birth rates and rural decline, a joint international research team from KAIST has developed a new data-driven model that incorporates the decline in the agricultural workforce into analysis of future food security (the ability to stably produce and supply food required by the public).

phys-org.title: Hidden electric space waves are quietly cleaning Earth's 'killer' electrons
phys-org.description: High above our heads, a silent battle is unfolding within Earth's magnetic shield. For decades, scientists have tracked "killer electrons"—ultrafast particles capable of piercing satellite armor and endangering astronauts as they zip through the Van Allen radiation belts. While we knew these dangerous particles eventually leak out of the belts and into the atmosphere, the primary mechanism "cleaning" the highest-energy electrons has remained a persistent mystery of space weather.

phys-org.title: Real-time microscopy reveals how semiconductor nanowires grow, and how bismuth seeds can speed their formation
phys-org.description: Scientists from the National Graphene Institute at the University of Manchester and Sun Yat-sen University have captured the growth of semiconducting tellurium nanostructures in liquid in real time, revealing how tiny seed particles form, grow into nanowires and compete for material as the structures develop.

phys-org.title: Perfectly preserved pterosaur wing rewrites the fossil rulebook
phys-org.description: An international study led by Curtin University has revealed new insights into how an ancient flying reptile was preserved in extraordinary detail for 113 million years, offering a rare glimpse into a vanished world.

phys-org.title: World's highest-consuming 10% cause up to $5.7 trillion a year in environmental damage, study finds
phys-org.description: The environmental damage caused by the world's highest-consuming 10% of people is worth $1.7 trillion to $5.7 trillion a year. At the central and upper estimates, this is several times more than the international community has committed to spend on climate action and biodiversity conservation combined, and is on the scale of the funding estimated to be needed globally to address these crises.

phys-org.title: How do flocking birds and schools of fish move? New research offers crystal-clear answer
phys-org.description: Flocking birds and schools of fish are a familiar sight. While previous research has uncovered the broad dynamics driving these movements, their underlying intricacies remain a mystery. Now a study by a team of New York University mathematicians offers new insights into these phenomena. It reveals that flocks and schools behave in ways similar to a soft crystalline material, with individual birds and fish serving as "atoms" that are evenly spaced in a lattice-like formation.

phys-org.title: Long-dismissed moss gene suppresses twins and triplets, reshaping ideas of plant evolution
phys-org.description: A moss gene previously thought to have been inactive actually plays a key role in its evolutionary success, researchers from the University of Bristol have discovered. The new paper published in Current Biology investigated a family of plant genes called WOX genes—proteins that help control growth and development.

phys-org.title: Early-career scientists build national infrastructure to bridge science and policy
phys-org.description: A new Special Report in the journal BioScience introduces the Scientist Network for Advancing Policy (SNAP), a student-led, nonpartisan, grassroots coalition founded in 2025 to empower early-career researchers to engage with science policy, advocacy and public communication. The report details the ways in which SNAP is reshaping the role of scientists in their communities.

phys-org.title: Orangutans eat medicinal plants in patterns that suggest self-medication
phys-org.description: Orangutans seek out plants with antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory and wound-healing properties, new research shows. Based on 20 years of observations of orangutans in Indonesian Borneo, scientists assessed how often the animals ate plants with known medicinal benefits. The findings, published in Scientific Reports, suggest orangutans eat combinations of plants in specific sequences—consistent with "self-medication" seen in other species.

phys-org.title: Q&A: Do high-pressure environments encourage moral disengagement?
phys-org.description: Why do individuals and organizations sometimes rationalize decisions that conflict with their stated values? According to Leah P. Hollis, professor of education policy studies in the Penn State College of Education, the answer may lie in "moral disengagement"—a psychological process through which people justify actions that might otherwise conflict with ethical or institutional standards.

phys-org.title: Study yields new insights on what makes conversation engaging
phys-org.description: What makes a speaker engaging? Both what is said and how it is said matter, but in different, complementary ways, a new study conducted at the McGill School of Communication Sciences and Disorders has found.

undark.title: Making Sense of Data From Wearable Health Trackers
undark.description: Wearable health devices such as smartwatches, glucose monitors, and sleep trackers are blurring the line between consumer wellness and clinical medicine. One physician argues that validation standards and privacy protections must be established to ensure the usefulness of the data these devices generate.

undark.title: In California, a Plan to Help Wildlife Cross a Busy Freeway
undark.description: The 101 freeway in California bisects a mountainous region where threatened cougars and other animals are blocked without a viable path across 10 lanes of heavily trafficked roadway. But an ambitious 210-foot “vegetated bridge” will soon be home to what organizers say is the largest wildlife crossing anywhere in the world.

undark.title: Promising ‘Liquid Biopsies’ May Not Be Ready for Primetime
undark.description: Multi-cancer early detection tests seek to spot cancer from a single blood draw. Enabling earlier cancer diagnoses could help save lives and limit the need for invasive interventions. But while the tests are promising, physicians have expressed doubt about routine use by low-risk and asymptomatic individuals.

undark.title: Book Review: How Radio Astronomy Made the Invisible Visible
undark.description: According to astronomer Emma Chapman’s revelatory “The Echoing Universe,” the history of radio astronomy is filled with surprises that have revealed parts of the universe that would otherwise remain hidden and invisible — DIY instruments, secrets accidentally uncovered, and persistent connections to Earth.

undark.title: Risk Aversion in Science Stifles Innovation
undark.description: Does the scientific enterprise play it too safe? C. Brandon Ogbunu argues that risk-taking in science involves a willingness to reflect on the processes and incentives of the profession — and to dramatically overhaul them if they do not work. Only then can true scientific innovation take shape.

undark.title: A Peptide, a Secretive Scientist, and a Debate Over Evidence
undark.description: Access to unapproved peptides like BPC-157 has become a cause célèbre for the MAHA movement. Undark contributing editor Sara Talpos digs into the untold history of BPC-157 and its long journey from the scientific margins to the center of a debate over U.S. drug regulation.

undark.title: Book Review: Within Our Cells, the Miracle of Constant Mutation
undark.description: Our cells are constantly mutating in a battle for the survival of the fittest that is raging inside us daily, Roxanne Khamsi writes in “Beyond Inheritance.” Many of these mutations are harmless, others are cellular deviants that lead to disease, and remarkably, some can actually self-correct.

undark.title: The Six-Week Postpartum Checkup Comes Too Late
undark.description: In the U.S., maternity care generally ends with a checkup scheduled six weeks after giving birth. This single doctor’s appointment may be efficient for billing and discharge protocols, but the timing reflects the structure of the health care system more than the reality of maternal recovery.

undark.title: Book Review:  The Case for Making Data-Driven Decisions
undark.description: In “Beyond Belief: How Evidence Shows What Really Works,” science journalist Helen Pearson profiles a group of people working in medicine and other fields who became leaders of the worldwide evidence movement, which encourages the use of data from rigorous research to direct treatments, policies, and plans.

undark.title: What the Hantavirus Story Reveals About Medical Mistrust
undark.description: The reaction to an outbreak of hantavirus on a cruise ship reveals a story about mistrust in medicine and public health. In the U.S., hantavirus disproportionately kills Native Americans. A doctor who works at a hospital on Navajo Nation writes that such mistrust always lands hardest on the most vulnerable.

public-dom.title: Louis Pope Gratacap, A Curator in Lost Worlds
public-dom.description: Arguably the first work of fiction to feature a *Tyrannosaurus rex*, Louis Pope Gratacap’s *The New Northland* (1915) is at once kaleidoscopic, mischievous, fascinating — and exhausting. Richard Fallon explores this “lost world” novel, finding a work as interested in cutting-edge science as it was in paying dues to its generic precursors.

public-dom.title: The Art of Kite Flying (1430–1929)
public-dom.description: 69 images of kite flying from across 5 centuries and some 10 countries.

public-dom.title: Venetian Bridge Brawls in 17th and 18th Century Art
public-dom.description: Paintings from an era when Venetians brawled on bridges.

public-dom.title: Genevieve Stebbins’ Delsarte System of Dramatic Expression (1886)
public-dom.description: A philosophical system and a practical guide for the cultivation of dramatic genius.

public-dom.title: The Launch of Our Mid-Year Fundraiser!
public-dom.description: Our Mid-Year Fundraiser is launched, and the new postcards theme will be Soil.

public-dom.title: Covers from Cerîde-i Adliye, a Turkish Law Journal (1924–26)
public-dom.description: Legal infographics that reflect a Turkish nation in flux.

public-dom.title: Animal, Vegetable, Lamb: The Zoophyte from Tartary
public-dom.description: In the Middle Ages, rumours spread across Europe of a strange hybrid creature, half-animal, half-plant, known as the Vegetable Lamb of Tartary. A hoax based on fern rhizomes? A euphemism for culled fetal lambs? Or perhaps a medieval misapprehension of cotton? Thom Sliwowski traces the roots of this fabled zoophyte.

public-dom.title: Harold A. Taylor’s Autochromes of California Flowers (early 20th century)
public-dom.description: Photographs of flowers by an advocate of California’s beauty.

public-dom.title: The Prophecies of the Brahan Seer (1877)
public-dom.description: Historical predictions from the Scottish Nostradamus.

public-dom.title: “Plaything of the Gods”: Photographs of Pushball (early 1900s)
public-dom.description: Photographs and films of a forgotten pastime.

public-dom.title: Twilight of the Velocipede: Typesetting Races before the Age of Linotype
public-dom.description: Before Linotype revolutionised typesetting in the 1880s, compositors set texts by hand — and they set them *fast*. Alex Wright rediscovers the thrilling world of typesetting races, which drew crowds in the thousands, offered huge cash prizes, and helped women "Swifts" fight for workplace equity.

public-dom.title: Diagrams from Willem ten Rhijne’s De Acupunctura (1683)
public-dom.description: A Dutch physician’s encounter with acupuncture.

public-dom.title: Longitude by Way of Wounded Hounds: Kenelm Digby’s Sympathetick Powder (1669 edition)
public-dom.description: A treatise on a powder that can cure wounds at a distance.

public-dom.title: Pyramid of the Capitalist System (1911)
public-dom.description: The working class undergirds everything in this cartoon of capitalist society.

public-dom.title: Magic by Return of Post: How Mail Order Delivered the Occult
public-dom.description: What allowed occultism to blossom in the United States at the turn of the 20th century? Linotype machines, cheap pulp paper, and newly improved postal networks. Allan Johnson investigates the forgotten history and (still living) world of mail-order magic.

public-dom.title: Pulex irritans: The Attack of the Monster (1885)
public-dom.description: Lantern slide of man battling bug.

public-dom.title: “A Beautiful Purplish Hue”: Frank Dudley Beane’s Experience with Ergot and Cannabis Indica (1884)
public-dom.description: An early contribution to drug literature, in which a man came to be fashioned out of wood.

public-dom.description: Announcing an exciting new book series!

proj-syn.title: AI Sovereignty Is About Options, Not Ownership
proj-syn.description: The US government’s abrupt decision to suspend foreign access to Anthropic’s Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models clarifies what “AI sovereignty” is really about. In the emerging AI economy, competitive advantage will come not from owning a single model, but from being able to evaluate, select, and orchestrate many models.

proj-syn.title: The Promise and Peril of AGI
proj-syn.description: Artificial general intelligence could dramatically increase human prosperity and free people from countless mundane tasks. But unless its benefits and ownership are broadly shared, it could deprive billions of workers of their livelihoods and pave the way for a new form of techno-authoritarianism.

proj-syn.title: Reversing Brexit Is Labour’s Best Hope
proj-syn.description: When it comes to the relationship between the United Kingdom and the European Union, political expediency and economic logic both point in the same direction. A majority of British voters now believe that Brexit was a mistake, and they are looking for a leader who will put the issue back on the national agenda.

proj-syn.title: Global Health Reform Must Bolster Innovation
proj-syn.description: As funding falls for global public health, calls for a country-led system have grown louder. Such reforms are necessary, but they must not come at the expense of new vaccines, medicines, and diagnostics, which can be delivered by strengthening mechanisms—such as product development partnerships—that already work.

proj-syn.title: Learning from the Right Sovereign Wealth Funds
proj-syn.description: The Gulf has made establishing a sovereign wealth fund seem like a strategic—and glamorous—choice, leading countries like Canada to launch their own. But Latin America has run this experiment many times over the years, offering a more realistic view of an SWF’s pitfalls and promise.

proj-syn.title: Europe Cannot Afford Another Lost Year
proj-syn.description: European businesses need simpler rules, faster permitting, affordable energy, stronger infrastructure, and a fully functioning single market. The longer that European policymakers fail to deliver on these policies, the greater Europe’s competitiveness challenge will become.

proj-syn.title: White House Fight Night
proj-syn.description: The venue on the South Lawn for UFC Freedom 250 was built, approved, lit, filmed, defended, watched, and enjoyed as part of a celebration of freedom. President Donald Trump’s chosen object to represent that celebration was a cage.

proj-syn.title: The US-Iran Agreement Is a First Step
proj-syn.description: While the recently announced US-Iranian memorandum of understanding is certainly good news, it is not definitive. The path from a statement of diplomatic intent to a fully restored, non-inflationary energy supply chain is fraught with political, technical, and physical risks.

proj-syn.title: Developing-Country Risk Is Being Mispriced
proj-syn.description: When investors say there are no “bankable” projects in developing economies, they are typically referring less to project quality than to the cost of capital. But the assumptions driving up risk premia are not supported by the evidence, and until this changes, the misallocation of capital will continue to undermine development.

proj-syn.title: The Fed Has Been Honest and Stupid
proj-syn.description: It would be easy—and a mistake—to blame the US Federal Reserve’s many blunders on corrupt bureaucrats or imagined conspiracies. The truth of the matter is that the central bank relies on an outdated regional map and lagging indicators that no longer tell the whole story, while battling macroeconomic blazes that politicians stoke.

proj-syn.title: A New Framework for Climate Displacement
proj-syn.description: Global warming is already uprooting communities and impoverishing people who remain in vulnerable areas—a crisis that is often overshadowed by the focus on decarbonization. But the Global Climate Mobility Principles offer policymakers a framework for ensuring that these individuals maintain their agency and rights.

proj-syn.title: Peace With Iran Is All About Lebanon Now
proj-syn.description: US President Donald Trump says that he "calls the shots" on negotiating with Iran, and Israel has no choice but to submit to a deal that undermines its security interests. But a deal that makes Trump the protector of Lebanon—and, by extension, Iran-backed Hezbollah—could put the US and Israel on a collision course.

proj-syn.title: Every British Prime Minister’s Nightmare
proj-syn.description: The true nature of Britain’s “special relationship” with the United States has far more to do with American financiers’ willingness to keep borrowing to purchase British government debt than with history, culture, or Britain’s defense needs. Every UK Prime Minister must bear this burden, which is rapidly becoming unsustainable.

proj-syn.title: India’s Unfinished Reform Agenda
proj-syn.description: Elevated oil prices, potentially strong El Niño conditions during the monsoon season, and the tariff-induced fragmentation of global trade are bearing down on the Indian economy and will likely be a drag on GDP growth. But these adverse conditions may be a blessing in disguise if they force India to complete its economic reform agenda.

proj-syn.title: The Middle East’s New Normal
proj-syn.description: The most likely outcome of the Iran war is not peace but an unsatisfying ceasefire that leaves the underlying issues unresolved. This will mean an uneasy equilibrium in which Gulf countries go their own way, US influence wanes, and the regional order remains unsettled.

proj-syn.title: No Bridge Over Healing Waters for the G7
proj-syn.description: The French G7 presidency’s focus on global imbalances is both welcome and problematic. While long-standing trade imbalances between the United States, Europe, and China are, if anything, becoming even more troublesome, the leaders’ summit in Évian-les-Bains will do nothing to address the problem.

proj-syn.title: Are Government Stakes the Key to AI Sovereignty?
proj-syn.description: At first glance, reports that the US and Chinese governments are both considering taking stakes in national AI champions would seem to suggest a convergence between the world’s two leading AI powers. But a closer look reveals stark differences in their underlying strategies.
